43: “Well, you are not the same as you were before,” I continued. “Once upon a time any one could see that you were our equal in everything, and that you loved us like relations, just as we did you; but now you are always serious, and keep yourself apart from us.”
42: “ Am I so odd?” said Katenka with an animation which showed me that my question had interested her. “I don’t see that I am so at all.”
40: “But you have changed tremendously since Woloda and I first went to Moscow. Tell me the truth, now: why are you so odd?” My tone was resolute.
34: “Oh yes, I am listening. You said that you danced—?”
32: “Yes. It is a pity you were not there. There were heaps of guests—about a thousand people, and all of them princes or generals, and there was music, and I danced—But, Katenka” I broke off, “you are not listening to me?”
30: “And you said, didn’t you, that once there was ever such a ball at Grandmamma’s?”
29: “Nothing, I only said that—” “No. You said, ‘Who knows whether we—‘”
28: Katenka stopped short, and once again became thoughtful. “What?” I asked with some anxiety.
26: “All the same, I am afraid of her. Besides, who knows whether we—”
24: “No, she only seems like that at first. She is grave, but not bad-tempered. On the contrary, she is both kind and cheerful. If you could only have seen the ball at her house!”
22: “But Mamma says that your Grandmamma is so very grave and so easily made angry?”
19: “Yes, of course. We shall have one half of the upper floor, and you the other half, and Papa the wing; but we shall all of us dine together with Grandmamma downstairs.”
13: “Yes, he said that we should all live there.”
11: “Did your Papa tell you that we girls too were going to live at your Grandmamma’s?”
0: “Well, but how large do you imagine? As large as Serpukhov?”
